meta.title: Who really said "Beware the leader who bangs the drums of war in order to whip the citizenry into a patriotic fervor"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Shakespeare and not Julius Caesar. It is an anonymous internet composition first seen in late 2001 — famously misquoted by Barbra Streisand in 2002.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Beware the leader who bangs the drums of war in order to whip the citizenry into a patriotic fervor'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Shakespeare, not Caesar — an anonymous online fabrication from late 2001, popularized during the run-up to the Iraq War and misquoted by Barbra Streisand.

answer.label: Not Shakespeare — an anonymous modern fabrication
answer.sourceLine: This line appears in no play by Shakespeare and in no ancient source for Julius Caesar. Fact-checkers can find no record of it before it surfaced on the Internet in late 2001, and its author is unknown. It is written as a fake first-person confession by “Caesar,” which is how it came to be pinned on both Caesar and Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar.

source.heading: Where it really comes from

docMeta.dd: None — not found in any Shakespeare play or Roman source
Summer 2002; recited by Barbra Streisand, 29 Sept 2002

source.excerpt: Beware the leader who bangs the drums of war in order to whip the citizenry into a patriotic fervor, for patriotism is indeed a double-edged sword. It both emboldens the blood, just as it narrows the mind. … the citizenry, infused with fear and blinded by patriotism, will offer up all of their rights unto the leader and gladly so. How do I know? For this is what I have done. And I am Caesar.
trail: Snopes ↗ rates it false: the words appear in no Shakespeare play and no history of Caesar, and “no record of this quote has been found prior to its appearance on the Internet in late 2001.”
Wikiquote ↗ files it as a misattribution to Julius Caesar, first seen online in late 2001, author unknown.
A Shakespeare specialist at Shakespeare Geek ↗ confirms the line is in none of the plays and cannot be traced before 2001.
In 2002 Barbra Streisand ↗ recited it as Shakespeare, then conceded after Matt Drudge exposed it that it was an anonymous internet composition.
source.excerptNote: The full circulating text is written as a first-person speech ending “And I am Caesar” — a modern pastiche, not a passage from any edition of Shakespeare.

sourceLink.text: Snopes: Julius Caesar and Drums of War

source.rightsNote: The wording has no identifiable source or first-publication date — it is an anonymous text that surfaced online around late 2001 — so its copyright status cannot be responsibly asserted. It is certainly not a public-domain passage of Shakespeare, since it appears in none of his works.

author.name: Anonymous (unknown author)
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.bio: Despite the confident attributions to Shakespeare and to Julius Caesar, no one has ever identified who wrote these lines. They first appear in online postings in late 2001 and spread through newsgroups and letters to editors during 2002, in the anxious run-up to the Iraq War. The text is deliberately styled as an ancient warning — ending “And I am Caesar” — which lent it a false pedigree it never earned.

misattribution.heading: How it got pinned on Shakespeare
misattribution.intro: The line is written to sound like an old warning, so it collected two prestigious but false authors — the historical Julius Caesar and Shakespeare’s play about him.

items.why: The words appear in no edition of Julius Caesar or any other Shakespeare work; a Shakespeare specialist and Wikiquote both confirm it is absent from the canon ↗ and untraceable before 2001.
No history of Rome or biography of Caesar contains these lines; Snopes ↗ notes the text was simply written in Caesar’s voice to borrow his authority.

At a Democratic gala on 29 Sept 2002 she read the passage as Shakespeare; after Matt Drudge exposed it she acknowledged, per contemporary reports ↗, that it was an anonymous composition — “whoever wrote this… should be writing their own play.”

misattribution.truthLine: There is no genuine author to restore: the line is an anonymous modern fabrication ↗ from late 2001, not Shakespeare and not Caesar.

context.heading: Why it caught on
lead: The quote surged in 2002 as the United States debated invading Iraq. Cast as a timeless warning from a fallen conqueror, it gave anti-war sentiment an air of ancient authority — which is exactly why it travelled so fast and why a careful reader should distrust it.
Its language gives it away: words like “patriotism” and “citizenry” and the whole rhetorical frame are modern, not Elizabethan, and certainly not Roman.
context.detailsSummary: A note on the Göring echo
detailsBody: The sentiment resembles a genuine, separately documented remark by Hermann Göring at Nuremberg (recorded in Gustave Gilbert’s 1947 Nuremberg Diary) that leaders can drive reluctant people to war by invoking attack and branding pacifists unpatriotic. That real quotation is often paired with this fake one, but the two are distinct: the “drums of war” wording is not Göring’s either.
context.pull: Written in Caesar’s voice to borrow his authority — but written no earlier than 2001.
